nameStory: Wild parsnip gets its name from the Latin 'pastinaca,' which comes from 'pastinum' meaning a two-pronged dibble tool used for planting. The root's long, tapered shape resembles this ancient gardening implement. This is the same species as the parsnips you'd find in the grocery store, just gone wild and feral in the New England landscape.
description: Wild parsnip is a tall, sturdy plant that can reach 2-5 feet high, belonging to the carrot family. In its first year, it forms a low rosette of divided, feathery green leaves, much like a carrot top. If left to grow a second year, it sends up a thick, grooved stem topped with flat clusters of tiny yellow flowers. The whole plant has a strong, earthy smell similar to cultivated parsnips when crushed.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flat-topped clusters (umbels) of tiny yellow flowers, like yellow Queen Anne's lace, blooming in mid-summer on tall stems

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided, feathery leaves with toothed edges that feel somewhat rough to the touch and smell earthy-sweet when crushed

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: First year forms a low rosette, second year shoots up a thick, deeply grooved stem that feels sturdy and hollow

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, oval, pale brown seeds with papery wings that flutter in the breeze, appearing in late summer

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Thick, angular stem with deep vertical grooves that you can feel with your fingers, often purple-tinged at the base

habitat: Wild parsnip thrives in disturbed soils along roadsides, field edges, abandoned lots, and waste areas throughout New England. It prefers full sun and well-drained soil, often appearing in the same spots where other weedy members of the carrot family grow. You'll commonly find it mixed with Queen Anne's lace, chicory, and other roadside plants.

seasonality.spring: First-year plants emerge as low rosettes of feathery leaves, while established plants send up their flowering stalks.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time when the distinctive flat yellow flower clusters bloom from June through August.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen to pale brown and disperse, while leaves begin to yellow and die back.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely, leaving only dried brown stems and seed heads that may persist into early winter.

funFact: Wild parsnip was so valuable in medieval Europe that it was used as a sweetener before cane sugar arrived—imagine sweetening your tea with parsnip syrup! However, this innocent-looking plant packs a dangerous punch: its sap contains chemicals that make your skin extremely sensitive to sunlight, potentially causing severe burns and blisters that can last for months.
confusionNotes: Wild parsnip is often confused with Queen Anne's lace, but remember: 'Yellow fellow, don't say hello'—the yellow flowers are your warning sign to stay away, while Queen Anne's lace has white flowers and is much safer to handle.
contextualKnowledge: This is the exact same species as the parsnips sold in grocery stores, just growing wild and free. European settlers brought parsnips to America as a food crop, but some escaped cultivation and naturalized throughout the continent, becoming both a useful wild edible and a potentially dangerous weed.
compareHints: Wild parsnip is the only parsnip species commonly found wild in New England. It's most easily confused with other carrot family members like Queen Anne's lace (white flowers, more delicate) and poison hemlock (white flowers, purple stem spots, much more toxic). The yellow flowers and deeply grooved stem help distinguish wild parsnip from its white-flowered relatives.
